# The Weight of the Water

Marcus is twenty-six years old, broad-shouldered and weathered in the way that men who work the sea tend to be, with callused hands and a squint that has less to do with the sun these days than with the effort of staying present. He has been fishing the North Atlantic with his father and uncle since he was seventeen, and until three years ago, the sea was the one place where he felt entirely himself.

It happened during a working trip abroad — a contract job off the coast of a country he had been warned was complicated but had gone to anyway, because the money was good and he was newly engaged and trying to build something. He was taken from the docks by men he did not know, held for eleven days in a concrete room he could not see out of, and subjected to things he still cannot bring himself to name in full. He describes it in fragments: cold water, the smell of cigarettes, sounds he made that he did not recognize as his own voice. He was eventually released without explanation, flown home by people from an embassy he had never contacted, and told by someone in a suit that it was over now.

It was not over.

Marcus married his fiancée, Lena, eight months after coming home, because the wedding had already been planned and he did not know how to explain why it should be postponed. He went back to fishing because it was what he knew, and for a while the physical exhaustion of the work seemed to help — hauling lines, mending nets, the cold spray on his face. But the sea began to change on him. The confinement of the boat's lower quarters became unbearable. He stopped going below deck unless absolutely necessary, and when he had to, he moved quickly, his chest tight, his breath coming in shallow pulls. His crewmates noticed but said nothing, the way fishermen do.

At home, Lena says he is somewhere else even when he is sitting across from her at the dinner table. She is right. He replays things — not in the clean, sequential way of a memory but in sudden, total immersions that arrive without warning. The smell of a particular brand of cigarette in a petrol station sent him to his knees in the car park last spring. He stood there for several minutes before he could locate himself in the present. He did not tell Lena about that.

He sleeps badly and briefly. When he does sleep, he wakes from dreams that leave a physical residue — his heart hammering, his shirt soaked, a certainty that something is still happening to him. He lies in the dark and listens to Lena breathe and tries to remember that he is in his own house, in his own country, that the walls are not concrete. Some nights it takes a long time.

He has become careful about control in ways that sometimes embarrass him. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks the locks on the house door twice before bed, then once more after Lena is asleep. On the boat, he is alert in a way that exhausts him — scanning the horizon, reading the other crew members' faces for shifts in mood that might mean something is wrong. He knows, on some level, that this vigilance is not rational. He does it anyway.

What Marcus finds hardest to say, and has only recently begun to approach in words, is that he feels ashamed — not of what was done to him, exactly, but of who he became in that room. He is not sure those two things are separable. He loves Lena and believes she loves him, but he holds himself at a slight remove from her, as though full closeness might require her to see something he is not ready to show. He keeps working. He keeps going out on the water. He is not sure whether that is resilience or simply the only thing he knows how to do.
